SourceActivities: 1.3 Can You Make a Perfect Copy?
Rights: Independent first-party prompt and rubric, no publisher activity artwork reused
OriginalFirstPartyTask: Start with two distinct points J and K. (a) Draw a circle centred at J through K and label another point L on the circle. (b) Explain why JL=JK. (c) A classmate guesses the midpoint M of JK by looking at the diagram and claims JM=MK. Explain why this is not a valid guarantee and replace the guess with a straightedge-and-compass procedure. (d) Show a labelled diagram and give a written justification. Use a paper construction or a separately verified tool; a working drawing app is not currently claimed.

Criteria.Criterion: Marks distinct points R and S, a circle centred at R through S and another point T on that circle.
Correctly justifies RT=RS as radii of one circle, independently of visual appearance.
Explains why an eyeballed N on RS does not ensure RN=NS, and may give an unequal counterexample.
Gives two equal-radius arcs with common opening strictly greater than RS/2, labels both intersections and the perpendicular-bisector midpoint.

FirstPartyCoolDown.Prompt: Given two distinct points R and S, draw a circle centred at R through S and label another point T on it. Which length equality is guaranteed? A peer points somewhere near the middle of RS and calls it N. Can they conclude RN=NS? Explain how to locate the true midpoint with permitted construction moves.
FirstPartyCoolDown.Exemplar: RT=RS because both are radii of the same circle. RN=NS is not guaranteed for a point chosen by sight. Draw equal-radius arcs from R and S using a common opening greater than RS/2, mark both intersections, then connect them to construct the perpendicular bisector; its intersection with RS is the midpoint.
FirstPartyCoolDown.TeacherScoring: Use criteria R1–R4 above; do not auto-score the sketch.

ReviewCases.Submission: Both congruent arcs intersect twice; their joining line crosses JK at midpoint M; circle JL=JK
ReviewCases.Disposition: Eligible for full rubric credit after teacher sees drawing

ReviewCases.Submission: Unlabelled sketch with no identified centres or compass opening
ReviewCases.Disposition: Request labelled evidence; cannot independently verify construction

ReviewCases.Submission: J and K coincide or arc radius equals JK/2
ReviewCases.Disposition: Degenerate or tangent case: cannot establish two distinct arc intersections

ReviewCases.Submission: Use intersecting arcs of any equal radius strictly greater than JK/2; either side ordering

NumericalSubcomponentOnly.Example: JK=8; each midpoint half-length 4 when midpoint is actually constructed
NumericalSubcomponentOnly.WrongExample: Estimated midpoint at distance 3 from J gives JM=3 and MK=5

SourcePedagogicalCaveat: The source 1.2 STARTS with estimated C on AB, circle A through B and circle B through C, produces triangle ADE and compares nonidentical student drawings before critique/repair. Preserve this intentional error exploration; digital tool availability is optional, paper allowed.

SupplementaryTeacherScoredTasks.Prompt: With centre O, a circle of radius 4 cm and a marked point A, first sketch a six-sided shape by eye. Then construct a regular hexagon on the circle by stepping compass opening OA around in one consistent direction, label the six consecutive vertices A through F, and explain why the six sides are equal and why the construction closes after six steps. Compare the freehand and constructed results.

Criteria.Criterion: Six distinct, consecutively labelled vertices on the correct circle
Unchanged compass opening OA used for each consecutive chord, with correct tool description
Each central triangle is equilateral, so all six chords equal OA
Six 60-degree central angles close one full turn; comparison with freehand sketch is justified

SupplementaryTeacherScoredTasks.Equivalence: Either clockwise or counterclockwise labelling accepted; rotations and reflections of a valid construction accepted.
SupplementaryTeacherScoredTasks.Reject: Freehand resemblance alone does not certify any equality.
SupplementaryTeacherScoredTasks.Delivery: Paper with teacher-reviewed drawing; digital tool is NOT a prerequisite and is NOT claimed live

Items.Prompt: A circle has centre U and radius UV. A second point W is on the same circle. Explain which lengths must match without measuring.
Items.Expected: UV=UW; each is a radius of the circle.

Items.Prompt: A circle is centred at C and passes through D and E. Decide whether CD=CE follows, and whether DE=CD necessarily follows.
Items.Expected: CD=CE always; DE=CD is not guaranteed without additional constraints.

Items.Prompt: On a 10 cm segment JK a student estimates M at 4 cm from J. Is M the midpoint? Explain, and give one guaranteed construction method.
Items.Expected: JM=4 and MK=6, so M is not the midpoint. Equal-radius arcs centred J,K with radius >5 cm give a perpendicular bisector.

Items.Prompt: A circle centred at C goes through A and D. A,C,D lie on one line in that order, and E is another point on that circle. Compare CE with AD. Explain without a ruler.
Items.Expected: CA=CD=CE as radii. With C strictly between A and D, AD=AC+CD=2CE. Thus CE=AD/2.
